content: The studies presented provide detailed insights into the detection and management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and related conditions, focusing on various diagnostic approaches, population subgroups, and geographical settings. 1. Between 2011 and 2015, in Papua New Guinea, a study conducted in antenatal clinics exclusively involving pregnant women (n=765) used PCR testing to identify cases based on symptoms alone. The results showed 30 true positives, 145 false negatives, 136 false positives, and 454 true negatives (Vallely et al.). 2. In the same period and country, another study in well-woman clinics (n=614) also relied on symptom-based PCR testing. The outcomes included 19 true positives, 27 false negatives, 181 false positives, and 387 true negatives (Vallely et al.). 3. A third study in Papua New Guinea, conducted in sexual health clinics (n=385) with 100% female participants, used PCR testing based on symptoms alone. The results were 62 true positives, 16 false negatives, 220 false positives, and 87 true negatives (Cohen et al.). 4. In Kenya, a study involving 115 women presenting with pelvic pain lasting 14 days or less was conducted in sexual health clinics. Endometrial biopsy and PCR testing were used to diagnose pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). The findings included 42 true positives, 54 false negatives, and 55 false positives (Grio et al.). 5. In the United States, between 1998 and 2000, a study involving 403 women at hospitals, sexual health clinics, and ambulatory care sites excluded those with acute PID. Subclinical PID was diagnosed using endometrial biopsy and PCR testing, yielding 27 true positives, 44 false negatives, 46 false positives, and 286 true negatives (Wiesenfeld et al.). 6. Another U.S. study in 2013, involving 150 women diagnosed with PID based on ICD criteria (symptoms and examination), reported 31 true positives, 14 false negatives, 86 false positives, and 19 true negatives. The diagnostic approach was unclear (Woods et al.). 7. In Italy, between 1997 and 2001, a study of 5516 symptomatic women with PID used LCR testing with the Abbott LCx system. The results included 23 true positives, 22 false negatives, 1697 false positives, and 3774 true negatives (Grio et al.). 8. Syndromic management of genital ulcer disease (GUD) was evaluated as an alternative to laboratory diagnosis or treating all cases. This approach aims to identify and treat STIs based on symptoms and clinical signs. While etiological diagnosis is preferred, it is often inaccessible or unaffordable in resource-limited settings. 9. The global distribution, incidence, and prevalence of pathogens causing GUD vary widely by region and population subgroup. This variability impacts the predictive value of diagnostic tests and the effectiveness of syndromic management. 10. Syndromic management has limitations, including low specificity, which can lead to unnecessary treatment, stigma, and antimicrobial resistance. However, it may be acceptable in high-morbidity settings where undetected cases pose significant risks, such as syphilis. 11. The accuracy of syndromic management depends on clinician skill, experience, and the clinical setting. It is less effective in general populations with lower STI prevalence compared to specialized STI clinics. 12. Prompt treatment of herpes simplex virus (HSV) with antiviral agents within 72 hours of lesion appearance can reduce viral shedding and ulcer duration by 1–4 days. 13. Studies on the cost-effectiveness of syndromic management show mixed results. Treating all cases may be more cost-effective in settings with high morbidity and mortality from undetected STIs, despite the risk of overtreatment. 14. The certainty of evidence for test accuracy and management effects varies, with many studies relying on convenience samples and lacking randomization, limiting generalizability. 15. The WHO recommends syndromic management for STIs in resource-limited settings, but emphasizes the need for better training of healthcare providers and improved diagnostic capacity to enhance accuracy and reduce unnecessary treatment. These findings highlight the challenges and trade-offs in managing STIs, particularly in resource-limited settings, and underscore the importance of balancing diagnostic accuracy, treatment accessibility, and cost-effectiveness.
